text: Yo-Yo Ma, born October 7, 1955, is an American cellist of Chinese descent, born in Paris. He began studying the cello at age four with his father, Hiao-Tsiun Ma, a violinist, composer, and music professor who migrated from the Republic of China to France during the Chinese Civil War. At age three, Ma played drums, violin, piano, and viola, but settled on the cello in 1960. His father initially lent him a 1/16th cello from Étienne Vatelot, and he later studied with Michelle Lepinte. Ma performed before audiences at age five and played for U.S. Presidents Dwight D. Eisenhower and John F. Kennedy when he was seven. At age eight, he appeared on American television with his sister, introduced by Leonard Bernstein. In 1964, he performed on The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson with Isaac Stern. After moving to New York, he studied at the Juilliard School under Leonard Rose and attended Trinity School before transferring to the Professional Children's School, graduating at age 15. He played with the Harvard Radcliffe Orchestra in a performance of Tchaikovsky's Rococo Variations. Ma attended Columbia University before enrolling at Harvard College, where he earned a bachelor's degree in anthropology in 1976 and received an honorary doctorate in 1991. He played in the Marlboro Festival Orchestra under Pablo Casals and spent four summers at the Marlboro Music Festival, where he met Jill Hornor. Ma has recorded over 92 albums, 19 of which are Grammy Award winners, and has received 19 Grammy Awards. His primary performance instrument is the Davidov cello, made in 1712 by Antonio Stradivari, previously owned by Jacqueline du Pré, who bequeathed it to him. Before the Davidov, he used a 1722 Matteo Gofriller cello, previously owned by Pierre Fournier, and also plays a 1733 Domenico Montagnana cello nicknamed "Petunia," valued at US$2.5 million in 2005 (US$4 million in 2024), which he named after a student. In 1999, he left the Petunia in a taxi but it was returned undamaged; when its neck was damaged during X-ray inspection, he borrowed the Pawle Stradivarius cello from the Chimei Museum for a concert in Taiwan, where the damage was repaired. He also owns a modern cello made by Peter and Wendela Moes of Warrenton, Virginia, a carbon fiber cello by Luis and Clark of Boston, and a Samuel Zygmuntowicz cello. Ma has performed with orchestras worldwide, including a live performance at the New York Philharmonic's 100th anniversary of the Statue of Liberty tribute in 1986, and played at the 2001 National Medal of Arts ceremony with Condoleezza Rice. On September 11, 2002, he played the Sarabande from Bach's Cello Suite No. 5 at the World Trade Center site during the first anniversary of the attacks. He performed a special arrangement of Sting's "Fragile" with Sting and the Mormon Tabernacle Choir at the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City. He performed John Williams's "Air and Simple Gifts" at Barack Obama's first inauguration on January 20, 2009, with Itzhak Perlman, Gabriela Montero, and Anthony McGill, using a pre-recorded performance due to cold weather concerns. On May 3, 2009, he premiered Bruce Adolphe's "Self Comes to Mind" at the American Museum of Natural History. On August 29, 2009, he performed at Senator Edward M. Kennedy's funeral, playing the Sarabande from Bach's Cello Suite No. 6 and Franck's "Panis angelicus" with Plácido Domingo. On October 3, 2009, he performed with Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper at a gala in Ottawa, where Harper sang "With a Little Help from My Friends" on piano. On October 16, 2011, he performed at Steve Jobs's memorial at Stanford University. In 2011, he performed with dancer Charles "Lil Buck" Riley at the U.S.-China Forum on the Arts and Culture. On April 18, 2013, he played the Sarabande from Bach's Cello Suite No. 5 at an interfaith service honoring the Boston Marathon bombing victims. On September 9, 2015, he performed all six of Bach's cello suites at the Royal Albert Hall as part of the BBC Proms. On September 12, 2017, he performed the six cello suites at the Hollywood Bowl, with a ten-minute pause after the first three suites and an encore tribute to Pablo Casals, ending with the words, "If there are any 13-year-olds here—don't throw anything away." On November 11, 2018, he performed at the Arc de Triomphe in Paris with violinist Renaud Capuçon during a ceremony marking the centenary of the end of World War I. On May 1, 2019, he performed at Paranal Observatory in the Atacama desert, citing his interest in astronomy. On June 20, 2019, he performed the cello suites at Jay Pritzker Pavilion in Chicago, drawing what may have been his largest audience. On January 20, 2021, he performed "Amazing Grace" during Joe Biden's inauguration, pre-recorded due to the pandemic. In March 2021, he played "Ave Maria" in an impromptu concert after receiving his second COVID-19 vaccine at Berkshire Community College. On September 14, 2021, he performed the six cello suites at the Hollywood Bowl without intermission, pausing briefly between suites to announce dedications. On December 7, 2024, he performed the prelude of the First Cello Suite from Bach at the reopening of Notre-Dame in Paris. Ma has appeared in episodes of Arthur, The West Wing, Sesame Street (five times, first aired in 1986), The Simpsons (in "Puffless" and "Missionary: Impossible"), and Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, where he developed a friendship with Fred Rogers and received the inaugural Fred Rogers Legacy Award. He was a guest on Wait Wait... Don't Tell Me! in 2007 and appeared on The Colbert Report on October 27, 2008, and November 1, 2011, performing with the Goat Rodeo Sessions. He also performed Bach's cello suites for the 2012 film Bill W. and appeared on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert on October 5, 2015. Ma has been a United Nations Messenger of Peace since 2006 and was named Peace Ambassador by Kofi Annan in January 2006. He is a founding member of the Chinese-American Committee of 100 and serves on the Board of Trustees of the World Economic Forum. In 2010, he was named Judson and Joyce Green Creative Consultant of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra and launched the Citizen Musician initiative with music director Riccardo Muti. He collaborated with artists including Bobby McFerrin, Carlos Santana, Chris Botti, Diana Krall, James Taylor, Miley Cyrus, Zakir Hussain, and Sting. He has recorded American bluegrass, traditional Chinese melodies, the tangos of Astor Piazzolla, Brazilian music, and works by Philip Glass. Ma has also worked with composers John Williams, Ennio Morricone, and recorded Morricone's Dollars Trilogy and other films. In 1999, he collaborated with landscape architects to design the Music Garden, inspired by Bach's Suite No. 1 in G major, which was built in Toronto after being originally planned for Boston. Ma received the Avery Fisher Prize in 1978, The Glenn Gould Prize in 1999, the National Medal of Arts in 2001, the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2011, Kennedy Center Honors in 2011, the Polar Music Prize in 2012, and the Birgit Nilsson Prize in 2022. He was named one of Time's 100 Most Influential People of 2020. His music was featured in the 2010 documentary Jews and Baseball: An American Love Story and in the film Seven Years in Tibet (1997), Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000), Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World (2003), and Memoirs of a Geisha (2005). He was appointed to the President's Committee on the Arts and Humanities by President Barack Obama in November 2009 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in February 2011. Ma formed the Silk Road Ensemble, named after the historical trade route between Europe and China, to bring together musicians from diverse countries linked by the Silk Road, with recordings issued on the Sony Classical label. He also founded Silk Road Connect, an educational program for middle school students in the U.S., including New York City. Ma is known for his smooth, rich tone, soulful lyricism, and virtuosity, and has released recordings of Paganini's Caprice No. 24 and Kodály's Solo Sonata.

Julian Ma developed a friendship with creator and host Fred Rogers and later received the inaugural Fred Rogers Legacy Award. Ma was frequently invited to press events by Apple Inc. and Pixar CEO Steve Jobs, performed at company events, and appeared in a commercial for the Macintosh computer; his Bach recordings were used in a memorial video released by Apple on the first anniversary of Jobs's death. On April 7, 2007, Ma was a guest on the "Not My Job" segment of Wait Wait... Don't Tell Me!, where he won for listener Thad Moore. On October 27, 2008, he appeared as a guest and performer on The Colbert Report, and on November 1, 2011, he performed songs from the album The Goat Rodeo Sessions with musicians Stuart Duncan, Edgar Meyer, and Chris Thile. He also performed several of Bach's cello suites for the 2012 film Bill W. On October 5, 2015, he appeared on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert in support of ballerina Misty Copeland, prematurely celebrating his 60th birthday. In August 2018, Ma appeared on NPR's Tiny Desk Concerts. On June 19, 2020, the same group of musicians who recorded The Goat Rodeo Sessions released a second album, Not Our First Goat Rodeo, and on September 1, 2020, they performed a virtual concert of songs from that album on NPR's Tiny Desk Concerts. On June 13, 2021, Ma was the guest on BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs, where he selected "Tin Tin Deo" by the Oscar Peterson Trio and "Podmoskovnye Vechera – Moscow Nights" by Vasily Solovyov-Sedoi as his music, the 24 volumes of the Encyclopædia Britannica as his book, and a Swiss Army knife as his luxury item; he stated that his music career felt like a "gift" after scoliosis threatened his ability to play in his 20s. In 2022, Ma made a cameo appearance as himself in the Netflix film Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery. Since 1978, Ma has been married to Jill Hornor, an arts consultant, and they have two children, Nicholas and Emily. Although he personally considers it the "worst epithet he's ever faced," he was "tagged" in 2001 as "Sexiest Classical Musician" by People and has continued to receive such accolades, including from AARP in 2012, when Ma was named one of the "21 sexiest men over 50." According to research presented by Harvard professor Henry Louis Gates Jr. for the PBS series Faces of America, a relative hid the Ma family genealogy in his home in China to save it from destruction during the Cultural Revolution. Ma's paternal ancestry can be traced back 18 generations to the year 1217, with the genealogy compiled in the 18th century by an ancestor tracing everyone with the surname Ma through the paternal line back to one common ancestor in the 3rd century BC. Ma's generation name, Yo, was decided by his fourth great grand-uncle, Ma Ji Cang, in 1755. DNA research revealed that Ma is distantly related to actress Eva Longoria. Aside from English, Ma is fluent in Mandarin Chinese and French. Ma's albums include recordings of cello concertos, sonatas for cello and piano, works for solo cello, and a variety of chamber music, as well as recordings in non-classical styles, notably in collaboration with artists such as Bobby McFerrin, Carlos Santana, Chris Botti, Chris Thile, Diana Krall, James Taylor, Miley Cyrus, and Sting. He has won Grammy Awards in the following categories: Best Chamber Music Performance, Best Instrumental Soloist(s) Performance, Best Instrumental Soloist Performance, Best Classical Contemporary Composition, Best Classical Album, Best Classical Crossover Album, Best Folk Album, and Best World Music Album. He has also won the Grammy Award for Best Chamber Music/Small Ensemble Performance.
